title: Dysuria and Urethral Discharge - Urethritis
patient_instructions: You are a 25-year-old man attending your GP because of urinary problems. For the past 7 days you have had pain, burning and stinging when passing urine, and it is not improving. If asked: you also pass urine more often. About a week ago you had some discharge from the tip of your penis which settled on its own. You have NO fever, chills, nausea, vomiting or flank pain; no scrotal swelling, redness or testicular pain; no rashes, ulcers or lumps in the groin; no blood in urine; no weak stream, dribbling or feeling of incomplete emptying; no back-passage pain; no new soaps, creams or underwear. Sexual history (give this only once the candidate asks sensitively and offers confidentiality): you are sexually active, you have had multiple partners recently, your partners are female, you never use condoms, no prior STI diagnosis that you know of, no sex with sex workers, occasional alcohol. Ideas: you are worried you 'caught something'. Concerns: embarrassment and whether it is serious. Expectations: you want it sorted and to know if your partners need treating. Affect: awkward, worried, becomes more open when reassured about confidentiality.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP. A 25-year-old man presents wanting to discuss urinary problems. Task: take a focused 6-minute history including a thorough sexual history, then explain your provisional diagnosis and differentials to the patient. You should also indicate the investigations and management principles, including partner notification.
examiner_instructions: The KEY pass component is a thorough, sensitively-conducted sexual history (not one or two token questions) with an explicit confidentiality statement. Reward a structured dysuria history and a systematic differential screen (cystitis/pyelonephritis, urethritis, epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis, ureteric colic, balanitis, penile lesions). The likely diagnosis is acute urethritis, usually sexually acquired. Strong candidates broaden the organism list beyond Chlamydia/gonorrhoea to include Mycoplasma genitalium, Trichomonas and adenovirus, and - critically - arrange PARTNER NOTIFICATION/contact tracing and advise abstinence until treatment is complete and contacts treated. Investigations: first-pass urine NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea, plus full STI screen. Prompt if needed: 'What will you do about the patient's partners?'

criteria: Introduces self, gives a confidentiality/sensitivity statement before intimate questions
Explores dysuria: character, timing, discharge, urinary symptoms
Takes a detailed structured sexual history (activity, partners, gender, protection, type of sex, prior STI, risk behaviours)
Screens differentials: pyelonephritis, epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis, ureteric colic, skin/penile causes
States acute urethritis as the diagnosis with reasoning (dysuria, frequency, prior discharge, high-risk behaviour)
Broadens causative organisms beyond chlamydia/gonorrhoea (Mycoplasma genitalium, Trichomonas, adenovirus)
Explains why alternatives (cystitis/pyelonephritis, epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis) are less likely
Orders first-pass urine NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhoea and offers a full STI screen (HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B)
Arranges partner notification/contact tracing and advises abstinence until treatment completed and contacts treated
States empirical Australian treatment (doxycycline 100 mg BD 7 days for chlamydia/NGU; add ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat + azithromycin 1 g if gonorrhoea suspected)
Non-judgemental, confidential, patient-centred handling of a sensitive history
Clear lay explanation of diagnosis, checks understanding and addresses embarrassment

red_flags: Untreated gonorrhoea or chlamydia progressing to epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis or (in partners) pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility
Missed Mycoplasma genitalium (macrolide-resistant) causing persistent non-gonococcal urethritis that fails first-line therapy
Failure to arrange partner notification/contact tracing - ongoing transmission and reinfection
Reactive arthritis as a recognised complication of chlamydial/NGU urethritis
australian_guidelines: Therapeutic Guidelines / ASHM: treat urethritis empirically with doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days for chlamydia/NGU, and ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat plus azithromycin 1 g if gonorrhoea is suspected; test for Mycoplasma genitalium with macrolide-resistance testing when NGU fails first-line therapy.

ASHM Australian STI Management Guidelines: partner notification/contact tracing (patient-referral, provider-referral, or the Let Them Know service) is mandatory for any diagnosed or suspected STI, with empirical treatment of contacts and abstinence until treatment completed.
RACGP: offer a full symptomatic STI screen (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B) and confirm/complete hepatitis B immune status.
learning_objectives: Take a structured dysuria history and a thorough, sensitive sexual history.
Recognise acute urethritis and its contemporary causative organisms including Mycoplasma genitalium.
Order appropriate first-pass urine NAAT and a full STI screen.
Arrange partner notification/contact tracing and empirical Australian treatment.
Communicate sensitive sexual-health information confidentially and non-judgementally.
key_points: A confidentiality statement before the sexual history is essential and often scored.
Non-gonococcal urethritis includes Mycoplasma genitalium, Trichomonas and adenovirus, not only chlamydia.
First-pass (first-void) urine NAAT is the specimen of choice for chlamydia/gonorrhoea in men.
Partner notification and abstinence until treatment completed are core management components.
A positive dipstick with pyuria but negative routine culture (sterile pyuria) should prompt STI testing.

citations.claim: Serious not-to-be-missed infective causes of dysuria/urethral discharge include gonorrhoea, chlamydia, Mycoplasma genitalium and herpes simplex, and reactive arthritis is a recognised complication.
Symptomatic STI screening/testing schedule (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B) and confirming immune status underpin the recommended full STI screen.
Any patient with urethral discharge requires a full sexual history and, if an STI is suspected, referral for full assessment and contact tracing.
Genital chlamydia is a documented cause of urethritis and of sterile pyuria, reinforcing that a positive dipstick with pyuria and negative routine culture should prompt STI testing.
